module_title: More Tools for Building AI Applications
review_basis: Original numbered R2 slide imagery 33-41 confirmed via runner spatial OCR; narration follows displayed comparisons and release/rollback diagrams.
part_title: CodePipeline Troubleshooting, CodeBuild, CodeDeploy and MLflow

scenes.title: Find a failed pipeline stage
scenes.narration: Let's start with a pipeline that hasn't completed. At the top, Source has succeeded, Build has failed, and Deploy has not started. That is useful information: the deployment isn't broken; it hasn't received a successful build yet. Follow the four numbered troubleshooting steps across the middle. First, open the failed action details and read the reason, stage and execution information. Second, inspect CodeBuild logs to find the actual error. It could be a missing dependency, a failing test or a command that can't find the expected file. Third, correct the buildspec or dependency configuration that caused the failure. Fourth, retry the failed stage or the pipeline and verify it genuinely succeeds. The optional notification flow at the bottom uses an EventBridge rule to detect pipeline state changes and alert the team. But notifications aren't the fix; they help people discover failures promptly. The lesson is to troubleshoot the first failed stage, use its logs as evidence, fix the root cause and only then allow later stages to proceed.

scenes.title: CodeBuild compiles and tests
scenes.narration: This slide separates building an application from deploying it. Follow the upper flow. A source repository provides application code and a buildspec file. CodeBuild starts a temporary build environment, runs the buildspec commands, installs dependencies, compiles the application and executes automated tests. If the tests pass, it packages the resulting artifact and sends logs and output to the configured destinations. If a test fails, the build stops and there is no valid artifact to promote. Look at the small result example: twelve tests passed, so packaging can continue. Now compare the two descriptions at the bottom. CodeBuild is responsible for turning source into a tested, packaged output. A deployment service consumes that output and installs it in a staging or production environment. That separation matters for AI applications too. Tests may validate API schemas, prompt templates, model configuration and expected safety behavior without deploying every attempted change. Build environments are ephemeral, so anything that must survive the build should go into the artifact or an appropriate external store.

scenes.title: Read a buildspec.yml
scenes.narration: Here we are reading an actual CodeBuild buildspec file, not just its name. Start at the top with version zero point two, which identifies the buildspec format. Under env, APP ENV is set to production, illustrating how environment variables are made available to commands. Move down to phases. The install phase uses npm c i to install dependencies reproducibly. The build phase runs npm run build. The post-build phase creates an output directory and copies the compiled files into it. Finally, the artifacts section lists output slash double-star and appspec dot y m l. Those are the files CodeBuild should collect for later pipeline stages. Notice that printing a success message is not the same as producing the expected artifact. A missing output folder or incorrect artifact pattern can break deployment even when compilation succeeded. Also, never put real credentials in plaintext buildspec variables. Sensitive values belong in an approved secrets service with appropriate permissions. The key takeaway is that phases define what commands run, while artifacts define what the next stage receives.

scenes.title: CodeBuild environment decisions
scenes.narration: This slide asks three configuration questions before a build starts. First, choose the build environment. A managed runtime image is convenient for common languages and tools, while a custom Docker image lets you control specialised dependencies. Second, provide configuration securely. Ordinary environment variables can hold non-sensitive settings, but credentials and tokens should come from Secrets Manager or Systems Manager Parameter Store with least-privilege access. Third, decide whether the build needs VPC networking. A build that only downloads public dependencies may not need it. A build that accesses a private database or internal service may require the right VPC subnets, routes and security groups. Notice the output at the bottom: build logs go to a logging destination for troubleshooting, and build artifacts go to the configured artifact destination for later pipeline stages. Enabling VPC connectivity doesn't automatically give internet access, so check egress paths if the build must reach package registries. The practical lesson is to design the build environment, secrets access and network path together instead of treating them as unrelated settings.

scenes.title: CodeDeploy in-place vs blue/green
scenes.narration: This side-by-side diagram compares two deployment strategies. On the left is in-place deployment. The existing EC2 instances currently run version one, and CodeDeploy updates the application on those same instances to version two. That reuses the infrastructure but means each instance is modified during rollout. On the right is blue-green deployment. The blue environment keeps running version one while a separate green environment is prepared with version two. Once the green application is ready, the load balancer can switch traffic toward it. If the new version fails validation, retaining the old environment makes rollback simpler. Look at the arrows rather than just the labels: in-place changes the software on existing machines; blue-green changes which environment receives production traffic. There are trade-offs. Blue-green generally needs capacity for both environments during the transition, but can reduce exposure to a bad release. In-place may use less additional capacity, though its rollback process requires more planning. Choose according to availability requirements, capacity and the application's ability to tolerate change.

scenes.title: Deploy Lambda with traffic shifting
scenes.narration: This slide illustrates a gradual Lambda deployment using CodeDeploy and a Lambda alias. On the left are two published function versions: the stable version one and the proposed version two. Clients invoke a production alias rather than hard-coding a version number. During the rollout, the alias sends most requests to version one and a small portion, such as ten percent, to version two. The diagram then increases the new version's share through intermediate percentages until it reaches one hundred percent. Why not switch everyone immediately? Look at the alarm branch below. Error-rate and latency metrics can reveal that the new function behaves badly under real traffic. If the configured alarm fires, CodeDeploy can stop the rollout and return the production alias to the stable version. Published Lambda versions are immutable, which gives the rollback a known target. Traffic shifting also means both versions must work with shared data formats while they run concurrently. The lesson is that controlled rollout plus monitoring is safer than replacing a production function in one unobserved step.

scenes.title: Deploy ECS with blue/green
scenes.narration: Now look at blue-green deployment for ECS rather than Lambda. The diagram starts with a healthy ECS task set running version one behind an Application Load Balancer's production listener. CodeDeploy creates or coordinates a green task set for version two. Health checks validate those new targets before users are shifted across. There may also be a separate test listener so the team can verify the green environment without changing production traffic. Follow the traffic arrow: after validation, CodeDeploy gradually moves production traffic toward version two while monitoring whether the new tasks stay healthy. If a health check or alarm indicates failure, the rollback path redirects traffic to the original task set. This resembles the previous slide, but the unit being deployed is different: here we are switching load-balanced container task sets rather than Lambda alias versions. Check target-group configuration, listener rules, deployment hooks and health checks when troubleshooting. A deployment isn't finished just because containers started; the new service must be ready to handle real application requests.

scenes.title: Release checklist for a GenAI API
scenes.narration: This slide extends a normal deployment checklist with the special risks of an AI API. Start at the top runtime path: a client calls API Gateway, Lambda processes the request, and Bedrock generates model output. Above that path is a separate model-configuration area containing the model ID, inference parameters, system prompt, guardrails and evaluation criteria. Those settings can change application behavior even without changing much code. Follow the release steps below. Implement request validation and error handling, build and test the handler, deploy a new version, then send representative prompts through the actual API. Check response structure, model quality and guardrail behavior, not just whether the endpoint returns HTTP two hundred. During rollout, monitor latency, errors, safety indicators and feedback. The decision diamond asks whether a threshold is breached. If it is, roll back to the previous safe version; otherwise continue monitoring. A key extra insight is that model responses are probabilistic, so regression tests should examine expected behavior and safety characteristics, not rely only on one exact string match.

scenes.title: MLflow for AI lifecycle tracking
scenes.narration: This slide introduces MLflow as a way to organise machine-learning experiments and the models that follow them. Across the top are four stages: record experiment runs, compare results, register a selected model and deploy it. In the first panel, multiple runs store parameters such as learning rate and batch size, metrics such as accuracy and loss, and artifacts such as model files or plots. The comparison panel shows that run two has the highest displayed accuracy, zero point eight seven six, so it is a candidate for promotion. A model registry records model versions and related governance information, while deployment makes an approved version available through an endpoint in an appropriate environment. Look at the lower adjacent capabilities: tracing can show what happened during an AI request, and evaluation can compare outcomes against a dataset. MLflow provides tracking and lifecycle tools; it doesn't by itself guarantee that a model is suitable for production. We still need validation, appropriate permissions and deployment checks. The big idea is reproducibility: knowing which data, parameters, metrics and artifacts produced the model we chose.
